gaps.sentence: The author ___ books sell millions worldwide lives in Iceland.
gaps.explanation: 'Whose' links the author to her books; 'who' could not be followed directly by 'books'.

gaps.sentence: He passed all his exams first time, ___ surprised everyone.
gaps.hint: refers to the whole previous clause
gaps.explanation: 'Which' can refer to a whole idea ('he passed first time'); this non-defining use never takes 'that'.

gaps.sentence: The people ___ moved in upstairs are very quiet.
gaps.explanation: 'Who' is the subject relative pronoun for people; 'whose' would need a noun after it.

gaps.sentence: It was the best meal ___ I have ever eaten.
gaps.hint: after a superlative, this pronoun is preferred
gaps.explanation: After superlatives ('the best ...'), 'that' is the preferred relative pronoun in defining clauses.

gaps.sentence: The exam, the results of ___ will be published on Friday, was very difficult.
gaps.hint: quantity noun + of + thing in a non-defining clause
gaps.explanation: 'The results of which' joins the clauses formally; 'of whom' is for people and 'of them' cannot link clauses after a comma.

gaps.sentence: Our new neighbours, ___ have three children, moved in last week.
gaps.hint: people as subject; clause between commas
gaps.explanation: 'Who' is used for people in non-defining clauses; 'which' is for things.

gaps.sentence: The police have arrested the man ___ stole the painting.
gaps.explanation: 'Who' is the subject relative pronoun for people in defining clauses.

gaps.sentence: The bridge ___ the campaign saved has just been listed as a monument.
gaps.explanation: 'Which' relates to the bridge, the object of 'saved'.
